Chapter 17, Śraddhātrayavibhāgayoga, the Yoga of the Threefold Division of Faith, opens with a question Arjuna carries over from the last chapter's teaching that scripture must be the standard for action: what of those who ignore scriptural injunction yet still sacrifice with real faith? Kṛṣṇa answers that faith itself is threefold, born of each person's own nature as sattva-, rajas-, or tamas-natured — and that a person, in the end, is what his faith is. He then traces this threefold pattern through one worldly domain after another: the gods, yakṣas, or ghosts each type of person worships; the food each finds appetizing, from the wholesome and nourishing to the bitter and overspiced to the stale and unclean; the sacrifice offered selflessly and by the rule, or for show, or without faith or form; the austerity of body, speech, and mind, practiced with detachment, for recognition, or out of delusion and malice; and the gift given to a worthy recipient without thought of return, or reluctantly for advantage, or with contempt at the wrong time and place. The chapter then turns to its most demanding teaching: the syllables Oṃ, Tat, and Sat are together the threefold name of brahman, by which the whole Vedic order of brahmins, scriptures, and rites was anciently established — Oṃ uttered at the start of every rite, Tat naming the renunciation of a rite's fruit, and Sat naming both existence itself and whatever is good, praiseworthy, or steadfastly pursued. The chapter closes by naming the opposite of all this: whatever is offered, given, or done without faith is asat, without worth, and avails nothing, neither in this world nor the next — faith, and not mere form, is what finally makes an act real.
